newsitem.title: JORDAN: Arafat, king share worries over Jewish settlements.
newsitem.headline: Arafat, king share worries over Jewish settlements.

text.p: Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and King Hussein agreed on Saturday that an Israeli drive to settle Jews in the occupied West Bank could undermine the Middle East peace process, Jordanian officials said.

"Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat expressed to King Hussein his deep worries of the dangers the declared policy to expand Jewish settlements in the West Bank poses to the peace process, which the king fully shares," a senior official said.

Underlining Jordan's improving ties with Palestinians as its relations with Israel deteriorate, officials said King Hussein gave Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat a presidential welcome when he arrived on the one-day visit.

The king and Arafat held brief private talks before joining their teams for a working lunch that another official said focused on the growing concerns over Israel's declared policy of expanding Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank.

"The visit of President Arafat is part of extensive efforts being exerted to get the peace process out of the crisis it is passing through," Information Minister Marwan Muasher told the official Petra news agency after the talks ended.

Arafat arrived from Gaza aboard a Jordanian helicopter that landed at Amman's Royal Raghdan Palace and was given a full guard of honour welcome by the king, Crown Prince Hassan and Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.

The Palestinian leader -- who has a history of uneasy relations with King Hussein -- is usually received with minimal pomp during his frequent short visits to brief the king on peace talks with Israel.
This welcome, a public show of support for Arafat in his negotiations with Israel, contrasted with a low-key reception on Thursday for visiting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.
Officials say the warm ties with Arafat reflect the king's growing exasperation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's policies, which the kingdom fears endangers its own stability.

Jordan, which had been Israel's closest friend in the Arab world, feels threatened by a Jewish settlement drive in the occupied Gaza Strip and West Bank, where some 140,000 Jews live in fortified settlements among over two million Palestinians.

Jordan fears it could spark violence that would spill over the border. Palestinians, who fled to Jordan after Israel's creation in 1948 and successive Arab-Israeli wars, are generally thought to form a majority of Jordan's population.
The ratio of "East Bank" and Palestinian Jordanians is one of the most sensitive issues in the kingdom and more Israeli pressure on Palestinians to move to Jordan could also fuel internal tensions.

Officials said Arafat told the king he would press a complain in the U.N.'s Security Council over Israeli plans to site Jewish housing in the middle of an Arab neighbourhood of East Jerusalem, captured by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in 1967.
Arafat also briefed the king on stalled talks with Israel over its long-delayed partial troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron. Clashes erupted in the town on Saturday.

Officials say Jordan fears Netanyahu's reluctance to honour existing peace accords with Palestinians could mean he would want changes in the 1994 Jordan-Israel peace treaty that demarcated their border for the first time.
